title: Tea Ceremony
tagline: A humble beverage becomes a philosophy of the mind.

scenes.text: Tang Dynasty China, 760 CE. A former orphan and court jester turned scholar sits alone in a bamboo pavilion. He lifts a bowl of green tea to his lips — and begins to write the work that will change how a civilization drinks.

scenes.speaker: Lu Yu
scenes.text: Tea is not merely a drink. The water must be spring water. The flame must be charcoal, not wood. The bowl matters. The moment of silence before drinking matters. Attention transforms the ordinary into the sacred.

params.title: Lu Yu’s Brazier
params.intro: Lu Yu’s brazier held wind, fire and water in balance. No recipe book here — only the cycle. Two things of one phase kindle the next phase. A thing fed by its mother phase grows one level. Pairs across the star clash and cost two attempts.
params.fact: In the Classic of Tea Lu Yu describes his cast-metal brazier: its windows bore the trigrams for wind, fire and water, because wind kindles fire and fire boils water, and one leg carried the words “its body balances the Five Phases and drives off a hundred ills”.

challenge.instruction: Water, flame and vessel must agree before the tea is made. Work the Five Phases as Lu Yu’s brazier did: wind kindles fire, and fire boils water.
challenge.fact: Lu Yu's Cha Jing (Classic of Tea, c. 760 CE) has 10 chapters covering tea's origins, tools for processing, making, drinking, and the history of tea. It transformed tea from a medicinal herb into a cultural art form.

scenes.text: Lu Yu's 'Classic of Tea' — the Chá Jīng — is the world's first monograph on tea. Written around 760 CE, it describes the plant's biology, cultivation, processing, and the philosophy of drinking. It created the aesthetic tradition of the tea ceremony.

challenge.instruction: Brew the tea in the Tang manner Lu Yu set down in the Classic of Tea. Put every step in its proper order.
challenge.fact: Lu Yu insisted on spring water collected before sunrise. He could allegedly identify which mountain spring water came from purely by taste.

scenes.speaker: Lu Yu
scenes.text: The Tang poets write of wine and longing. I write of tea and presence. To truly taste a cup of tea, you must be nowhere else. That is harder than most men imagine.

challenge.instruction: Lu Yu measured every cup. Combine the ingredients in the proportions shown, and leave out what belongs under the kettle, not in the bowl.
challenge.fact: Lu Yu says to season the water with a little salt at the first boil, to add the powdered tea at the second, and that one sheng of water makes five bowls. Too much water, he warns, and the flavour turns thin.

challenge.instruction: Lu Yu’s rules outlived the Tang: Song tea masters, and later Japan’s tea ceremony, prized iron-glazed tea ware. Give each part of the teapot its oxide, then fire the kiln.
challenge.fact: Tenmoku (天目) glazes — prized in Japanese tea ceremony — used iron oxide to create the signature oil-spot and hare's fur patterns in Song Dynasty kilns.

scenes.speaker: Lu Yu
scenes.text: Batu Khan waits at Krakow, but nothing is happening there, and without an event there is no fight. I will go first; the turn after I arrive, play the Miracle card on Krakow and we attack.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 3 · Starting an Event. Deploy Lu Yu to Krakow and End Turn. Next turn play the Miracle card there, add your follower and win one attack.
challenge.fact: Event cards start a scenario at a location where you already have a Great Person, and only one who arrived on an earlier turn can start it. A local event keeps running until a player ends it.
